sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures

items.q: The osteoporosis definition combines reduced bone ___ with disrupted bone ___.
items.exp: The page defines loss of bone strength in terms of low bone mass and impaired microarchitecture. (Book p895)

items.q: Assess the definition diagram: I Cortical bone loss is emphasized over trabecular loss. II Bone quantity alone fully describes bone strength.
items.exp: The diagram gives trabecular > cortical involvement and separately includes microarchitectural quality. (Book p895)

items.q: A postmenopausal woman has progressive back pain before a fragility fracture is recognized. Which distinction matches the source?
opts: Back pain is the earliest symptom; fracture is the characteristic manifestation
Fracture is always the earliest symptom; pain excludes osteoporosis
Tetany is the earliest symptom; back pain is unrelated
Bone pain requires high ALP and excludes osteoporosis
items.exp: The clinical tree labels back pain as earliest and fracture as the characteristic symptom. (Book p895)

items.q: The source's characteristic population is ___, with a quoted figure of ___.
items.exp: The source labels postmenopausal women (40%); the figure is not defined well enough to treat as a universal prevalence estimate. (Book p895)

items.q: Match the following source fracture clues — 1) Commonest site named 2) Axial compression site illustrated later 3) Sensitive male fragility marker … A) Vertebral body B) Femoral neck C) Distal forearm
items.exp: The page names femoral neck as most common, includes vertebral fractures and identifies distal forearm fracture as a sensitive male fragility marker. These source site rankings are not universal epidemiology. (Book p895)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among the chapter's common fragility-fracture sites?
items.exp: The source lists femoral neck/hip, vertebral and Colles fractures, not mandibular condyle fracture. (Book p895)

items.q: A woman has early menopause, smokes and exercises little. Which additional history strengthens the source's osteoporosis risk profile?
items.exp: Low estrogen, early menopause, smoking, low activity and low Ca/vitamin-D intake are listed risk factors, alongside female sex, family history and alcohol. (Book p895)

items.q: Assess risk modification: I Family history and female sex are listed risks. II Alcohol exposure and low physical activity are also listed.
items.exp: The page includes inherited/demographic and potentially modifiable exposures; they should not be treated as mutually exclusive groups. (Book p895)

items.q: Match the following drug-associated clues — 1) Pioglitazone 2) PPIs 3) Lithium … A) Nephrogenic DI/thyroid dysfunction B) Fluid retention/bladder-cancer warning C) Low Mg/tubulointerstitial injury
items.exp: These are the accompanying drug notes. Pioglitazone's bladder-cancer wording reflects a risk warning rather than certainty of causation in each user. (Book p895)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among medication risks for osteoporosis listed on this page?
items.exp: Teriparatide is an anabolic treatment discussed later; steroids, heparin and cyclosporine are in the risk list. (Book p895)

items.q: In addition to aluminum and common anticonvulsants, excess replacement with ___ is listed as a bone-loss exposure.
items.exp: L-thyroxine appears in the risk list; clinically the concern is excess thyroid hormone rather than appropriate replacement by itself. (Book p895)

items.q: A patient taking lithium develops high calcium with inappropriately elevated PTH. Which mechanism fits?
opts: Direct parathyroid destruction with low PTH
Renal PTH resistance with phosphate retention
items.exp: Lithium alters CaSR signaling and can cause hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia; this page's 'hypo' wording conflicts with that mechanism. (Book p895)
